prime.problem: A long run hits the context limit, the harness summarizes the past, and the agent carries on. If you treat that as housekeeping, a failing test can come out the other side as "tests passing", and nothing in the transcript tells you where the fact went.
prime.fits: The previous cards showed the working set is assembled per call and that snapshots trade freshness for stability. Compaction is the moment the harness rewrites that working set for good. It sets up the memory card (what must be written somewhere durable) and the capstone's question about false success claims.
expect: head and tail, summary request and continuation
the serialization cut (2,000 characters in OpenCode)
prime.goal: Given a compaction that lost a fact, name the boundary where it stopped flowing, and design a summary contract that carries status and open obligations verbatim.

attend: In OpenCode, why did the nested src/AGENTS.md rule never reach the summarizer, even though it reached an ordinary request?
Why do the global and root rules come back after compaction while the attached note does not?
Why does pytest's output layout make a head-only cut especially bad for test status?
What has to be true of the workspace for "flush before discard" to be enforceable?
If the full record is still on disk after compaction, in what sense has anything been lost?

must: History outgrows the window → the harness summarizes the older head and keeps the tail → later calls see only summary + tail → anything not carried into the summary is gone from every later request, even though storage still has it

The serializer cuts each old tool result to a fixed length before summarizing → anything appended late in a result (a nested rule, pytest's verdict line, an exit code) never reaches the summarizer → no summary prompt can recover it; only extracting it before the cut can

The summarizer sees a failure only as scattered evidence and writes a fluent one-line status → "failed" or "unknown" becomes "passing" (status inflation) → the final message repeats it → a false success claim the checker catches

Instruction files are reloaded by ordinary prompt assembly after compaction → rules in AGENTS.md come back → facts that lived only in the conversation (test results, user asks, decisions) do not → those are what must be flushed or pinned before the discard
elevated: Where the harness places an appended item inside a tool result (before or after the body) decides whether a head-only cut keeps it → OpenCode appended the nested rule after the file, so the cut dropped it
reference: OpenCode's exact continuation wording ("What did we do so far?", "Continue if you have next steps…")
Hermes's 28 → 12 active SQLite rows plus 28 compacted after /compress here 2
the paper figures (1,323 episodes; 0% → 30%; 53% and 10% rule survival)
OpenCode v1.18.30 and Hermes v0.20.1 version pins

compress.prompt: Card closed: draw the path a fact takes from a tool result to the call after compaction, mark the two places it can be lost, and in 3–4 sentences explain how the Tuesday run's "tests passing" summary happened and what would have prevented it.
checklist: path: tool result → history → head/tail split → serializer cut → summary request → summary → continuation (summary + tail)
loss 1: cut before the summarizer sees it; loss 2: seen but left out or rewritten by the summary
pytest prints its verdict and the exit code comes last, so a head-only cut drops them
"tests passing" is status inflation: failed upgraded to passed
prevention: extract and pin {cmd, exit, counts} before the cut (flush before discard), carry it verbatim, reread or rerun before claiming done

retrieve.q: Explain why Govindarajan calls compaction a state transition rather than housekeeping, using what a later call can and cannot see.
answer: it replaces what later calls are built from, not just what is displayed
later calls see summary + tail; the old records stay in storage but are no longer selected
so like any state mutation it needs a trigger, a commit point, recovery and observability

retrieve.q: Walk through OpenCode's compaction in the experiment: what goes into the summary request, what is cut, and what the continuation request contains.
answer: the older head is serialized as text; the most recent user turn is kept as the tail
completed tool results are cut to 2,000 characters, so the end of the old read and the appended nested rule are lost
continuation: a "What did we do so far?" user message, the summary, the retained tail, then a "Continue…" user message
ordinary instruction files are reloaded alongside it

retrieve.q: A colleague proposes fixing status inflation with a stronger summary prompt ("never claim tests pass unless you saw it"). What does that fix, and what can it not fix?
answer: it can reduce the summarizer rewriting a failure it did see
it cannot recover facts cut before the summarizer saw them (the verdict line, the exit code)
it is still a model judgment; pinning status from the full result before the cut is deterministic

retrieve.q: Hermes's database showed 12 active rows after compression, yet the recent tail still reached the next request. Which surface would you inspect to debug a "forgotten" fact, and why not just the database?
answer: the actual provider request (and the summary's input), because that is what the model saw
the active-row view differs from live selected history after compression
compare persisted history, live history and the outbound request to find where it stopped

compare.q: A read limit cuts a tool result when it is acquired; the compaction serializer cuts it later, before summarizing. What is fundamentally different about the two cuts, and how does each one fail?
answer: the read-time cut happens in the open: the model sees the truncated result at that step and can ask for more
the compaction cut is invisible to the model: it happens inside the summary request and later calls only see the summary
read-time cuts fail as missing detail the agent can notice; compaction cuts fail silently, which is how status can inflate

compare.q: Hermes's prompt snapshot keeps an old USER.md; compaction drops an old test result. Both make the model see something other than the current truth. What choice causes each, and which is easier to repair?
answer: snapshot: stale by design, for stability and caching; the durable file still has the truth and a rebuild brings it back
compaction: lossy by design, for space; if the fact lived only in the conversation there is no durable source to rebuild from
so compaction needs the flush-before-discard step and the snapshot does not

compare.q: Which link of the claim chain does the step-7 summary break, and why can't a checker that only reads the transcript after step 7 catch it?
answer: it asserts "command succeeded" when the command exited 1
after compaction the transcript the model sees contains the summary, not the exit code
the checker must rerun pytest or read the stored full step-6 result, i.e. check the world, not the summary

predict.q: The Compaction Cliff reports 53% of safety rules surviving one round of /compact and 10% surviving five. If each round dropped rules independently at the same rate, what would five rounds give? Is the reported 10% higher or lower, and what might that say?
predict.answer: Independent rounds: 0.53<sup>5</sup> ≈ 0.042, about 4%. The reported 10% is higher, which would fit rules that survive one round being likelier to survive the next (some rules are stickier). This is our arithmetic on the summarized figures, not the paper's analysis; check its methods before leaning on it.

apply.task: Open code/compaction-lossy.py. First change CAP to the smallest value that keeps the "1 failed, 41 passed" line, then change it back and instead move the [exit code: 1] line to the front of RESULT. Rerun both and record which facts survive.
apply.done: You found that a cap of 2,227 characters (2,208 + the 19 characters of "1 failed, 41 passed") keeps the counts but still cuts the exit code at 2,245, and that putting the exit code first makes it survive the 2,000 cap.
apply.hint: A fact survives only if all of its characters lie before the cap: start position + length ≤ CAP. When you prepend the exit-code line, every later position shifts by its 15 characters.
